quick_notes.detail: First step of British Government to control EIC. Made GG of Bengal. Established Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774). Prohibited EIC servants from private trade.
quick_notes.explanation: The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first law passed by the British government to control the East India Company (EIC), which was a British trading company that had begun ruling large parts of India. This act created the position of Governor-General of Bengal, meaning one person became the top British official for that region. It also established the Supreme Court in Calcutta (now Kolkata) in 1774, which was a high court that could hear cases and apply English law. quick_notes.title: Pitts India Act of 1784
quick_notes.detail: Distinguished between commercial and political functions. Created "Board of Control" (Political) and "Court of Directors" (Commercial) - System of Double Government.
quick_notes.explanation: The Pitts India Act of 1784 was a law passed by the British Parliament to fix problems in how the British East India Company ruled India. Before this Act, the Company did both business and government work, which caused confusion and corruption. The Act clearly separated these two jobs: it created a new group called the Board of Control to handle all political and military matters, and it kept the existing Court of Directors to manage only the Company's trade and commercial activities. This setup is called the System of Double Government, meaning two separate bodies controlled different parts of the Company's work. The Board of Control was made up of British government officials, including a minister, which gave the British government more power over Indian affairs. The Court of Directors remained in charge of buying and selling goods, but they had to follow the Board's orders on political decisions.

quick_notes.title: Charter Act of 1813
quick_notes.detail: Ended EIC's trade monopoly in India (except Tea and trade with China). Allowed Christian missionaries. 1 Lakh for education.
quick_notes.explanation: The Charter Act of 1813 was a law passed by the British Parliament that changed how the East India Company (EIC), the British trading company that controlled much of India, operated. Before this Act, the EIC had a trade monopoly, meaning it was the only British company allowed to trade with India, but the Act ended that monopoly except for two items: tea and trade with China, which the EIC kept exclusive control over. The Act also allowed Christian missionaries to enter India and spread their religion, which had been restricted earlier. Finally, the Act set aside one lakh rupees (100,000 rupees) from the Company's funds to be spent on education, specifically to promote literature, learning, and the introduction of Western sciences in India.

quick_notes.title: Charter Act of 1833 (Final Centralization)
quick_notes.detail: Made GG of Bengal as "GG of India" (Bentinck). Ended EIC as a commercial body. Attempted to introduce open competition for Civil Services.
quick_notes.explanation: The Charter Act of 1833, also known as the final centralization act, was a law passed by the British Parliament that made the Governor-General (GG) of Bengal the Governor-General of India, with Lord William Bentinck becoming the first person to hold that title. This act ended the East India Company's (EIC) role as a trading company, meaning it could no longer buy and sell goods for profit, and instead turned it into a purely administrative body that only governed British territories in India. The act also attempted to introduce open competition for the civil services, which meant that people could try to get government jobs based on their test scores rather than through family connections or by paying money, though this change was not fully put into practice at that time.

quick_notes.title: Charter Act of 1853
quick_notes.detail: Separated legislative and executive functions of GG Council. Introduced open competition for Civil Services (Macaulay Committee 1854).
quick_notes.explanation: The Charter Act of 1853 renewed the charter of the British East India Company. It separated the law-making (legislative) and law-executing (executive) functions of the Governor General's Council, meaning that for the first time a separate Legislative Council was created to handle only making laws. quick_notes.title: Government of India Act 1858
quick_notes.detail: Following 1857. Transferred power to Crown. GG title changed to Viceroy. New office "Secretary of State" created (Member of British Cabinet).
quick_notes.explanation: After the 1857 rebellion, the British government took full control of India from the East India Company (EIC), which was a private trading company that had ruled parts of India. This law transferred all powers of governing India from the EIC to the British Crown, meaning the Queen of England became the direct ruler. The title of the Governor-General (GG), who was the head of British administration in India, was changed to Viceroy, which means the Queen's representative. A new official position called the Secretary of State for India was created; this person was a member of the British Cabinet (the top group of ministers in London) and was responsible for making all final decisions about India. This act ended the Company's rule and started the period of direct rule by the British monarch, known as the British Raj.

lesson_intro: Today we study the 'Legal Framework of Empire'. The British didn't just rule by sword; they ruled by Law. We trace the evolution of constitutional acts from the Regulating Act of 1773, which first brought the Company under parliamentary control, to the Government of India Act 1858, which transferred power to the Crown. For UPSC, these acts are the foundation of both History and Polity (M. Laxmikanth Chapter 1). Focus on the 'Key Features' of each act—this is high-yield territory.
